stories.topic: The Schoolboy Who Timed Firecrackers Floor by Floor
stories.summary: At breakfast, Amit's friend Vaishnav told him about a boy at his school. On a festival day (Amit thinks it was Diwali), the boy went to the fifth floor with a homemade chain of strings and delayed-fuse firecrackers. He dangled one firecracker into the toilet on each floor below and timed them to go off in sequence. The fourth floor went off and the teachers ran up. When they got there, the third floor went off, so they ran there, then the second, and so on.
stories.insight: Amit sees mischief like this as raw initiative and creativity. Given real opportunity in the economy, the same kind of person can do amazing things. The question the episode keeps returning to is how India channels that energy into productive firms.
stories.quote: the first thought that came to my mind when Vaishnav told me the story is that these are the future of our country. This is innovation.

stories.topic: They Stole a Bridge in Bihar
stories.summary: Amit recalls his Seen and the Unseen episode on Bihar with Mohit Satyanand and Kumar Anand. Thieves stole an entire bridge: one day it was there, the next it was gone. The show notes link a report on a 60-foot bridge stolen in broad daylight. Before that, a patch of water had been stolen too; Amit calls it a river, and the show notes link a stolen pond. He adds that many big telemarketing scams are run out of a couple of towns in Bihar.
stories.insight: Amit says these stories are bad on one hand and good on the other, because they show potential. India has the imagination and the sheer numbers of inventive people to compete with anyone, and it is constraining itself. Ajay's reply is that the task is to channel this energy into firms.
stories.quote: You know, think of the innovation. People just stole a bridge. One day there was a bridge. It wasn't there. Only in Bihar.

stories.summary: Ajay recalls Sundar Pichai saying it will be a great day for India when a Bangladeshi immigrant becomes CEO of Infosys, just as Pichai, an Indian immigrant, became CEO of Google. Ajay argues India is too insular for that today: people would culturally resent a foreigner running a beloved company like Infosys or TCS. In the US, Satya Nadella at Microsoft and Pichai at Google were ordinary appointments that nobody protested as anti-foreign.
stories.insight: Amit's twist: so many American firms having Indian CEOs speaks to the greatness of America, not India. Being open to foreign talent at the very top shows whether a country puts building a great firm ahead of identity.
stories.quote: I remember Sundar Pichai once said that it will be a great day for India when a Bangladeshi immigrant becomes the CEO of Infosys.

stories.summary: Ajay retells a story Lant Pritchett often tells about South Korea's chaebols. It looked like crony capitalism: the government struck a political bargain with eight or ten big business houses and promised to create conditions for them to export. Because the goal was exporting, the Korean state had no way to rig the outcome. It could not make the American market easier, could not hurt American competitors, and could not help through protectionism.
stories.insight: Even a cosy state-business deal can drive productivity if the measure of success is one the state cannot fake. Making exports the goal pushed all of Korean public policy towards pro-productivity, pro-social behaviour.
stories.quote: So suddenly the entire channel of public policy goes in the correct direction. You go into pro-social, pro-productivity, sensible activities, because your purpose is exporting.

stories.topic: Indian Software Didn't Wait for the State
stories.summary: Ajay concedes that better education, health and electricity policy are good goals, but each is a 25-year journey that won't move the needle soon. TCS, Infosys and the other heroes of Indian software did not wait for the government to build colleges that would train a million programmers a year. They solved their own problems and kept their dealings with the Indian state to a minimum.
stories.insight: There is enough hunger and opportunity in India to make huge progress without waiting for the state to fix everything. The software industry's playbook is a can-do one: compete abroad, stay away from the state.
stories.quote: They didn't wait for the government of India to build engineering colleges where one million people will learn how to do programming every year. They just went ahead and solved their own problems.

recommendations.item: In Defense of Globalization
recommendations.creator: Jagdish Bhagwati
recommendations.context: Amit's recommendation for the episode. It came up right after Ajay credited Bhagwati and others with showing that exporting creates a healthier political economy.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a great, magnificent book that everyone should read. It is the natural companion to Ajay's case for globalisation.

recommendations.item: Graduating to Globalisation: A Study of Southern Multinationals
recommendations.creator: Dilek Demirbas, Ila Patnaik & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The paper the episode is named after. Amit notes that the term was coined by Ajay.
recommendations.reason: It studies outbound FDI, where hundreds of Indian companies now build factories and companies abroad. Ajay calls this a glorious and often overlooked mode of internationalisation.

recommendations.item: Export Versus FDI with Heterogeneous Firms
recommendations.creator: Elhanan Helpman, Mark J Melitz & Stephen R Yeaple
recommendations.context: On Ajay's reading list, which he offered instead of a book: a kit of research papers on firm internationalisation, many by other researchers in a field he says is opening up.
recommendations.reason: It addresses the exporting-versus-FDI question at the heart of the episode. Ajay argues the two are complementary, not a menu of choices.

recommendations.item: Exporting & firm performance: Evidence from India
recommendations.creator: Apoorva Gupta, Ila Patnaik & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: From Ajay's reading list on firm internationalisation.
recommendations.reason: Indian evidence on the episode's central link between exporting and how well firms perform.

recommendations.item: Export vs FDI in Services
recommendations.creator: Rudrani Bhattacharya, Ila Patnaik & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: From Ajay's reading list.
recommendations.reason: Takes the export-versus-FDI question to services, which matters given India's software and services exporters.

recommendations.item: India's Financial Globalisation
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah and Ila Patnaik
recommendations.context: First item on Ajay's reading list.
recommendations.reason: Background on foreign capital as a mode of internationalisation. Ajay argues Indian firms need foreign capital to match competitors' cost of capital.

recommendations.item: Motivations for capital controls and their effectiveness
recommendations.creator: Radhika Pandey, Gurnain K Pasricha, Ila Patnaik & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: From Ajay's reading list.
recommendations.reason: Relevant to his argument that restricting firms' access to foreign capital is as silly as restricting their access to imported coal.

recommendations.item: Did the Indian Capital Controls Work as a Tool of Macroeconomic Policy?
recommendations.creator: Ila Patnaik & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: From Ajay's reading list.
recommendations.reason: A closer look at India's capital controls, part of the state machinery Ajay criticises for its anti-foreign stance.

recommendations.item: Capital account openness in India and a comparison with China: Then versus now
recommendations.creator: Nidhi Aggarwal, Sanchit Arora & Rajeswari Sengupta
recommendations.context: From Ajay's reading list, one of the papers by other researchers.
recommendations.reason: Compares how open India is to foreign capital with how open China is, a useful backdrop to the episode's China-diversification point.

recommendations.item: Determinants of Trade Misinvoicing
recommendations.creator: Ila Patnaik, Abhijit Sen Gupta & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: From Ajay's reading list.
recommendations.reason: Part of his reading kit on how trade and money cross India's borders.

recommendations.item: The investment technology of foreign and domestic institutional investors in an emerging market
recommendations.creator: Ila Patnaik & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: From Ajay's reading list.
recommendations.reason: Looks at foreign equity capital, one of the modes of internationalisation discussed in the episode.

recommendations.item: Foreign Investors under Stress: Evidence from India
recommendations.creator: Ila Patnaik, Ajay Shah & Nirvikar Singh
recommendations.context: From Ajay's reading list.
recommendations.reason: Examines how foreign investors behave in India under stress, relevant to the foreign-capital thread.

recommendations.item: Foreign Currency Borrowing by Indian Firms: Towards a New Policy Framework
recommendations.creator: Ila Patnaik, Ajay Shah & Nirvikar Singh
recommendations.context: From Ajay's reading list.
recommendations.reason: Connects to his steel-mill argument that Indian firms need cheaper foreign debt to compete globally.

recommendations.item: From domestic to global asset pricing
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: From Ajay's reading list.
recommendations.reason: Part of his kit on what changes when Indian firms and capital become integrated with the world.

recommendations.item: Instant cross-border payments vs. current account inconvertibility
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah & Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah
recommendations.context: From Ajay's reading list.
recommendations.reason: Ties to his complaint that the Indian state treats cross-border activity as suspect.

recommendations.item: Cross-border activities in India need more freedom, not less
recommendations.creator: Pratik Datta & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: From Ajay's reading list.
recommendations.reason: Essentially the policy chapter's prescription in written form: the state's anti-internationalisation stance needs to go.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay refers to the Kelkar–Shah book while framing development as the emergence of high-productivity firms.
recommendations.reason: He says the book's whole approach to public policy asks one question: how do we create conditions in which entrepreneurs, managers, financiers, engineers and workers come together into sophisticated firms?

recommendations.item: Three Great Leaps by Firms (Episode 22 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit opens by framing this episode as part of a continuing body of work on firms.
recommendations.reason: Their first episode purely about firms: three firms that surprised and shocked them by how they changed.

recommendations.item: How Family Firms Evolve (Episode 34 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Named by Amit as one of two especially significant episodes in the firms series.
recommendations.reason: Amit says it contains novel, original thinking about how Indian firms evolved over 30 years, the kind of scholarship he wishes universities did.

recommendations.item: From Imperial to Adaptive Firms (Episode 37 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The other firms episode Amit singles out as significant.
recommendations.reason: Covers how Indian firms should keep evolving to suit a diverse country. Amit says it combines big-picture thinking with granular detail.

recommendations.item: Lant Pritchett Is on Team Prosperity (Episode 379 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit mentions it while promising a future episode on what's wrong with development economics. He brings it up again during the RCT rant.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a great recent conversation that went deep into development economics, including the triviality of many RCTs.

recommendations.item: Economic Learnings of India for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Bihar (Episode 345 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: The source of the stolen-bridge story.
recommendations.reason: His guests described the inventive things happening in Bihar, which Amit reads as evidence of India's untapped potential.

recommendations.item: They Stole a Bridge. They Stole a Pond
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes alongside the news reports of the Bihar bridge and pond thefts Amit narrates.
recommendations.reason: Amit's own piece on the thefts he uses to illustrate India's raw, misdirected ingenuity.

recommendations.item: The Brave New Future of Electricity (Episode 40 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay recalls that he and Amit have done a lot of thinking and talking about electricity policy.
recommendations.reason: Background for his point that fixing Indian electricity is a 25-year journey, which cannot justify subsidies for firms today.

core_ideas.concept: Development Is the Emergence of High-Productivity Firms
core_ideas.explanation: Every country has labour; the puzzle is getting more done per working hour, and that mostly happens inside firms. A firm brings together capital, labour, governance, technology, management and contracts. If a quarter of Indians worked in firms at the global frontier of productivity, India would be an advanced economy (though only a third of working-age Indians work today). Saudi Arabia and Qatar show the contrast: high income from selling gas, but without the firms, the knowledge or the changed society. Ajay calls real development a human story.
core_ideas.quote: So getting to high productivity firms is the necessary and sufficient condition of becoming an advanced economy.

core_ideas.concept: Development Economics Has Lost the Plot
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay argues the field got absorbed in philanthropy, aid, poverty and redistribution. It says surprisingly little about the world's great development successes: Taiwan, South Korea, Israel and Chile, poor in 1945 and advanced today. He wants researchers to study firm productivity, domestic political economy, and the causes and consequences of internationalisation. These questions can't be answered with randomised controlled trials, and he is proud of working on them anyway.
core_ideas.quote: I shall not allow my mind to be blinkered around one microscope.

core_ideas.explanation: A firm internationalises through imported inputs, exports, foreign capital (equity, from portfolio investment up to FDI, and debt), foreign employees, and building operations abroad. Policy economists often treat these as a menu to pick from. Ajay says they feed each other. Foreign workers know cheap vendors back home, and foreign shareholders and board members open doors to FDI in places like Brazil. Even imports reveal something: because local inputs are easier, firms import only highly specialised things.
core_ideas.quote: On any of the six dimensions you push forward in one dimension, it'll end up helping the other dimensions.

core_ideas.concept: Exporting Is a Market Test, Not a Revenue Game
core_ideas.explanation: Business people see exports as extra sales, but that is a fallacy of composition. When a whole country exports more, its currency strengthens, imports get cheaper and some domestic producers die. India's software exports pushed up the rupee and hurt manufacturing exports, which economists call Dutch disease. That is just Ricardian specialisation, and since imports and exports move together, the gap between them isn't a meaningful target. Exporting matters because passing a global market test proves a firm is world-class. It also opens a bigger market and economies of scale; for a global firm size signals quality, while for a local monopoly like Coal India it means nothing.
core_ideas.quote: The game is not to get revenues out of exports. The important point is exporting is passing a market test.

core_ideas.concept: Exporting Cleans Up a Toxic Political Economy
core_ideas.explanation: Domestic firms compete by turning a weak developing-country state against each other: favourable regulations, tax raids, and joint lobbying to keep foreigners out. The worst players can win, and they make the state worse. Ajay credits Jagdish Bhagwati, T. N. Srinivasan and Anne Krueger with seeing that exporting changes this game. No amount of lobbying in Delhi helps Infosys sell to Germany; only productivity does. Exporting firms also stop talking nationalism, because they want cheap foreign inputs.
core_ideas.quote: So even in a bad country, pressure of exporting brings out better behavior from the firms.

core_ideas.concept: Fake Exports: Subsidies and a Rigged Exchange Rate
core_ideas.explanation: A government can create the motions of exporting without the substance in two ways. It can hand out subsidies, such as PLI, or it can weaken the currency; at 100 rupees a dollar instead of 80, even inefficient firms can export. Either way the country confuses means with ends. The goal was never a billion dollars of exports; it was high-quality firms.
core_ideas.quote: What it was all about was high quality firms not that billion dollars of exports.

core_ideas.concept: You Can't Love Exports and Hate Multinationals
core_ideas.explanation: Modern production is spread across countries. An engine made in Brazil can be shipped to Madras, assembled into a car and sold in America. About 50% of global trade happens within firms, and smart firms ignore borders, choosing locations for low cost and for diversification. Harnessing exports means being deep inside the world of multinationals, both foreign firms coming in and Indian firms going out. George Fernandes-style irritation with multinationals, plus tax and rules-of-origin harassment, works directly against exporting.
core_ideas.quote: If you like exporting, you like multinationals. These are one of a piece.

core_ideas.concept: Mr. Capital: The Invisible Biggest Input
core_ideas.explanation: An engineer sees a steel mill as iron ore, coal, labour and imported machines. An economist notices the elephant in the room: capital. Its cost per ton of steel is bigger than any of those inputs. To compete with the best mills in Korea, Japan or America, an Indian mill must match their cost of capital. Foreign equity and debt are cheaper, partly because India is poor and partly because its financial system is bad. So openness to foreign capital is about competitiveness, not ideology.
core_ideas.quote: It is as silly to interfere with internationalized capital access as it is silly to interfere with internationalized coal access.

core_ideas.concept: Competition Punishes Prejudice, So Hire Nationality-Blind
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay cites George Stigler: a capitalist who discriminates against a minority is hurting herself. Successful firms care about getting things done, which gives capitalism a progressive social character. It brings people into voluntary contracts and 'double thank you' moments that are immune to prejudice. Amit adds that discrimination is costly only in a truly competitive market, and Ajay replies that exporting is that market. Refusing to hire foreigners is as wrong as refusing to hire Muslims or Dalits. Sometimes nationality is even an asset, such as Korean networks for selling into Korea.
core_ideas.quote: The consideration of the nationality of the job applicant should be deleted in the HR database at the point of application.

core_ideas.concept: Policymakers Should Kick Subsidy-Seekers Out of the Room
core_ideas.explanation: Every location has some cheap and some expensive inputs. Labour costs more in Brazil, and electricity is cheaper in Germany. India's bad electricity policy needs fixing, but that is a 25-year journey and no excuse for subsidies today. A factory with 20 workers using 20 megawatt hours of electricity a day probably belongs in Germany, because there is no Indian edge. The state should let firms choose where and what to produce. As Amit notes, most of what Ajay asks of the state is to get out of the way.
core_ideas.quote: So we should just kick the firms out of the room when they want a subsidy.

core_ideas.explanation: Indian civil servants and regulators, more so under populism, treat foreign engagement as bad by default. This covers foreign bank accounts, travel abroad, overseas subsidiaries, tax havens and running a business through Dubai. The reflex runs through SEBI, RBI, the ED, company affairs, income tax and GST. Only the largest firms can afford the compliance nightmare; smaller ones just give up. Ajay calls this the Indian state actively harming India's emergence.
core_ideas.quote: Okay, if you fly to London within 10 minutes, you will get a bank account opened. You suffer the misery of a foreigner coming to India trying to open a bank account.

core_ideas.concept: Is Your Skill Fixing India, or Being a Competent Firm?
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's strategic question for managers. A competent firm should look outward and keep dealings with the Indian state to a minimum, as the software industry did. Even if you are clean, competitors will turn the state against you. The world market is effectively infinite, so you can keep growing for 25 years, and it insulates you from India's ups and downs.
core_ideas.quote: Is my skill fixing the Indian system, or is my skill of being a competent firm? If you're a competent firm, look outside.

core_ideas.concept: Internationalisation as a Hard-to-Fake Metric for Boards and Investors
core_ideas.explanation: Boards can use internationalisation metrics to hold managers to account and look past quarter-to-quarter profit. These include export share and growth, assets abroad, access to global capital, foreign hires, specialised imports and the number of countries a firm operates in. Investors use the same test. A firm selling in the EU, UK or US has proved it is good, while a domestic winner might have won through state power. Amit calls this a 'fast and frugal heuristic'. Ajay applies it to Nitin Pai's three types of Indian IT firm: services exporters like TCS and Wipro and SaaS exporters are safe bets, domestic firms need more scrutiny.
core_ideas.quote: Those kinds of metrics are very hard to fake, and they are deeply connected to firm productivity.

core_ideas.concept: India's Quirky Rules Create Dwarf Firms
core_ideas.explanation: There is a subtler harm too. India's unusual web of SEBI and RBI rules, a government-monopoly identity system and UPI shapes firms around Indian peculiarities. Their systems and software then don't work in Bangladesh, Japan or America. Ajay also asks whether UPI is actually good, or whether it won because PayPal was blocked. You can't tell when success came behind protection.
core_ideas.quote: So it's a very subtle problem where policymakers are creating dwarfs

core_ideas.explanation: Amit draws on a distinction Ram Guha once made to him. Patriotism is loving your country. Nationalism is toxic, exclusionary, chest-thumping and macho, and it powers the demands for tariffs, subsidies and currency manipulation that keep firms mediocre. A patriot wants India to compete and win. Ajay adds a nuance: the import substitution of the 1960s and 70s wasn't toxic nationalism but analytical failure by deluded economists. Firms, though, always stand ready to ask for protection.
core_ideas.quote: I think what a true patriot will say is that no, that we have it in us to be as good as anyone in the world. Let us compete, we will get better, and we will show you what we can do.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit, deadpan, on Bihar's crime wave: "Like an entire bridge has been stolen from Bihar. You know, think of the innovation. People just stole a bridge... Only in Bihar." He adds that the bridge went only after a patch of water had already been stolen.
Amit in role-play mode: "I'm a podcaster, what do I do? I'm kidding. Don't look at me like that... I'm a podcaster, I will podcast."

On RCTs: Ajay says you don't have to be an "RCT Nazi" to study big questions. Amit piles on: "I wouldn't be surprised if there's an RCT somewhere. That do people perceive a yellow shirt to be brighter than a black shirt? That's the kind of rubbish they are doing."
Amit on Ajay's personified economic inputs: "In a previous episode, gentle reader, you met Mr. Gas. Today you have met Mr. Capital." He says these characters reveal Ajay's "interior landscape".
Ajay's summary of what exporting demands of Infosys, since lobbying Delhi can't win German customers: "Like shut up and do your goddamn job better."
Ajay mocking economists who treat modes of internationalisation as a menu: "Do I want this, do I not want this? He loves me, he loves me not."

I18N: Ajay explains that early computing ran in English on 127 ASCII characters. When software had to support Korean, Japanese and other languages, "computer scientists were very lazy in typing", so 'internationalization' became I + 18 letters + N.
George Stigler's argument that a capitalist who discriminates against a chosen minority is actually harming herself.
George Fernandes, whom Ajay describes as "obsessively irritated about multinational corporations operating in India", a stance modern trade theory rejects.
Jagdish Bhagwati, T. N. Srinivasan and Anne Krueger, who drew on India's failure in the 1960s and 70s to show that exporting produces a different, healthier political economy.
Dutch disease: Indian software exports pushed up the rupee and hurt manufacturing exports. Ajay calls it Ricardian trade theory at work and "part of life".
ASML, TSMC and Sony as firms to admire and study: "What is the magic of ASML? What is the magic of TSMC? What is the magic of Sony?"
China under Xi Jinping: global firms realised they were overexposed to China and rushed to diversify. Ajay: "Sadly, not much has happened in terms of Indian gains out of this process."
Taiwan, South Korea, Israel and Chile, poor in 1945 and advanced today, as the great development stories. Ajay notes the OECD hasn't admitted Taiwan, yet it is "a first-class advanced economy".
Amit borrows the idea of 'fast and frugal heuristics' (one or two simple rules for a complex problem) and proposes a firm's level of internationalisation as one.
Amit riffs on a classic line: "No man is an island, no mode of internationalization, I18N, is an island either."
